True.

The Indian Constitution made the provision of the right to vote for adults. All the provisions of the pre-independence period which restricted the right to vote were cancelled after independence, and the Constitution guaranteed adult suffrage by giving the right to vote equally to both men and women above the age of 21 years. The voting age was later reduced from 21 to 18, which gave the young generation an opportunity for political participation. Such provisions have made India the largest democracy in the world, and India has the largest number of voters compared to any other democratic nation.

False.

The Right to Information has had exactly the opposite effect. Citizens have a right to know about the functioning of the government, and the Government of India gave the Right to Information to the citizens to ensure transparency and accountability, which are the hallmarks of good governance. The Right to Information has made the government more transparent and has reduced the element of secrecy in the working of the government. It also increases communication between citizens and the government, which helps in strengthening democracy and in building a relationship of trust between them.

True.

The Constitution is dynamic and is seen as a living document, because it has to change according to changing conditions. The Parliament has the power to make those changes, and the judiciary has accepted this power of the Parliament to amend the Constitution. At the same time the judiciary has specified the limitations on this power and has taken the stand that while amending the Constitution the Parliament cannot alter the basic structure of the Constitution. So the Constitution can grow and adapt with time while its basic framework stays protected.

In the decades after independence progress was made towards more and more democratisation of India, but in that process the citizens were considered only as beneficiaries of what the government did for them. In the last few decades development has instead come to be considered as the right of the citizens. This is the rights based approach. After the year 2000 the whole approach towards democratic reforms changed in this way, and democratic reforms began to be considered as 'rights' of citizens. Accordingly, citizens in India have got the Right to Information, education and food security, and these rights have strengthened democracy in India.

Citizen empowerment is the essential condition of democracy, and citizens have a right to know about the functioning of the government. The Government of India gave the Right to Information to the citizens of India to ensure transparency and accountability, which are the hallmarks of good governance. The chapter refers to it as RTI 2005. It has made the government more transparent and has reduced the element of secrecy in the working of the government. It also creates opportunities for the citizens' participation and interaction with the government, and this increased communication helps in strengthening democracy and in building a relationship of trust between citizens and government.

In our country, from the very beginning, women have had inadequate representation in politics and political institutions. The chapter's chart of the representation of women in the Lok Sabha shows this clearly: there were 22 women MPs (4.50%) in the 1951-52 election, the number fell to its lowest of 19 (3.51%) in 1977, and it rose to its highest of 66 (12.15%) in 2014. So even at its best the share of women has stayed low. Many countries in the world have made efforts to increase the representation of women, and changes are taking place in India as well: the 73rd and 74th amendments reserved 33% of the seats for women in local self-governing institutions, and this percentage has been raised to 50% in several states including Maharashtra. The chapter also observes that if the family structure, social surrounding, economic sector and political sphere become more open, women will get a chance to participate in decision making, and that for this purpose women's participation should be increased in the representative institutions.

[Note: the reservation of 33% and 50% mentioned in the chapter is for local self-governing institutions; the chapter does not state any reservation of seats for women in the Lok Sabha.]

The Constitution had first guaranteed adult suffrage to both men and women above the age of 21 years, and the voting age was later reduced from 21 to 18. The main effect of this was that it gave the opportunity of political participation to the young generation in India. Along with the other provisions for adult suffrage, it has made India the largest democracy in the world, with the largest number of voters compared to any other democratic nation. This change is not only quantitative but also qualitative, because new political parties are emerging with the active support of young voters. These parties represent the various expectations of the people and compete in the political sphere.

Social justice and equality are important objectives of our Constitution, and the Constitution has given the guidelines to establish a new society based on these two values. To establish social justice is to remove those social conditions which are responsible for injustice and to insist on the equality of dignity for all individuals. The principles of justice and equality aim at ending discrimination in social status, such as treating people as superior or inferior on the basis of caste, religion, language and gender, place of birth, race and property, and at giving equality of opportunity for development to every individual. Efforts for this have to be made at all levels of society, but the government's efforts and policies on this front are more important. For democracy to be inclusive one must try to bring all sections of society into the mainstream, and democracy is in fact a process of accommodating different sections in society, which helps in reducing social conflicts.

The protection provided to the citizens by the fundamental rights in the Constitution has been made more meaningful through various decisions of the judiciary. Protection of the honour and dignity of women is one of the important subjects on which the Court has given such judgements; the others the chapter lists are the rights of children, protection of human rights, individual freedom and tribal empowerment. These efforts of the judiciary have made the political process in India more mature. The chapter itself asks students to find out the judgements given by the Supreme Court on these subjects in recent years and to discuss them.

[Note: the chapter does not name any particular court decision or case; it only states that the Court has given judgements on the protection of the honour and dignity of women. The Act for the protection of women against domestic violence, which the chapter says underlined the need to protect the dignity and self-esteem of women, is a law and not a decision of the Court.]
